note: Part B (drawing) is not transcribed: no model answer exists.

questions.text: A 12cm x 12cm x 12cm wooden cube is painted and its four views are shown below. This cube is sliced into 64 smaller equal sized cubes of 3cm x 3cm x 3cm. How many of these small cubes will have exactly one green face and exactly one orange face in the same cube?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The first view shows three faces meeting at one corner, all orange, and the third view shows three faces meeting at another corner, all green. So the cube has three orange faces around one corner and three green faces around the opposite corner. A small cube has exactly one green and one orange face only if it lies on an edge where an orange face meets a green face, and is not a corner cube. There are 6 such edges, each with 4 small cubes of which 2 are not corners, so 6 x 2 = 12.

questions.text: The following figure is cloned and the cloned figure is reflected along the XY axis. How many rectangles are present in the resultant figure?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Reflecting the clone about XY gives a symmetric figure: a tall rectangle, a column of three squares, a mirrored column of three squares and a mirrored tall rectangle. Count every rectangle whose four sides are drawn lines (squares included), working through each pair of vertical lines and each pair of horizontal lines that both span between them. Counting systematically over every pair of vertical lines and every pair of horizontal lines gives 25 rectangles.

questions.text: Shown below are pieces of a regular polygon. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Every corner visible on the pieces turns the edge by about 51 degrees, so each interior angle is about 129 degrees. A regular polygon with n sides has exterior angle 360/n, and 360/7 is about 51.4 degrees. So the polygon is a heptagon with 7 sides.

questions.text: How many different types of characters appear in the figure given below?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Turn the grid so the characters stand upright and go through it row by row, listing each character the first time it appears. Look closely at near twins: a character with and without a hook, a mark on top or a crossbar is two different characters. IIT Bombay's final key gives 28 types.

questions.text: How many fonts are used in the given set of words?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Group the words by the shapes of their letters, not by size: compare the contrast between thick and thin strokes, the ends of strokes, the shape of the curves and the headline. A word in a heavier weight or a different style of the same design still counts as a separate font if its letters are drawn differently. IIT Bombay's final key gives 11 fonts.

questions.text: A shopkeeper is offering discounts for the festive season. The discount is based on a series. The following table depicts the first five combinations of this series. The purchase amount and discount are in rupees. How much is the discount for a purchase of Rupees 75,000?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The lower limits 151, 301, 601, 1201, 2401 are \(150 \times 2^k + 1\), so each slab doubles. The discounts 19, 49, 109, 229, 469 rise by 30, 60, 120, 240, so the discount is \(30 \times 2^k - 11\). Rs 75,000 lies in the slab from 38,401 to below 76,801, which is k = 8. The discount is \(30 \times 256 - 11 = 7669\).

questions.text: Given the following equation, how many parrots are equal to one elephant?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Write P for a parrot, F for a fish and E for an elephant. The first line gives P + 2F = 4E. The second gives 2P + E = F + P, so F = P + E. Substituting, P + 2P + 2E = 4E, so 3P = 2E and one elephant equals 1.5 parrots.

questions.text: How many of the alphabets using the font shown below when flipped on the horizontal axis, can still be read as capital alphabets in the same font?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Flip each letter about a horizontal line through its middle and ask whether the result still reads as a capital letter of the same font, either the same letter or another one. Letters whose top and bottom halves mirror each other stay the same, and in this font some letters turn into others when flipped. IIT Bombay's final key gives 11 letters.

questions.text: Shown below in figure 1 is a layout of a chess board with one knight and several pawns. Given that the knight cannot land on any square that has a pawn, but can jump over it, the pawns cannot move, and the knight moves on a chess board as shown in figure 2, what is the least number of steps required for the knight to reach square x?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The knight moves in an L shape and may not land on a pawn square. The ring of pawns blocks most direct routes, so search outward from the knight one move at a time. Number columns 1 to 8 and rows 1 (top) to 8. The shortest route is (row 8, col 5) to (7,3), (5,2), (3,1), (1,2), (2,4), (4,5), (2,6) and finally x at (1,4): 8 moves. The only squares a knight can reach x from are (2,2), (2,6) and two pawn squares, and a search shows no route of 7 or fewer moves.

questions.text: Shown below is a fan with red coloured patterns on it. When it rotates, the patterns make circles. How many red circles will be seen when the fan rotates?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: When the fan spins, each red mark sweeps a ring at its distance from the centre, and marks at the same distance on different blades merge into one ring. Measuring the distance of every red mark from the hub centre gives separate bands: the petal ring and the thin ring on the hub, then six bands along the blades (some made by marks on two or three blades together). That is 8 red circles in all.

questions.text: Figure 1 has been constructed by overlapping some alphabets. Assuming the alphabets may be rotated, how many alphabets from figure 2 cannot be overlapped to fit within figure 1?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A letter can be overlapped onto figure 1 only if every stroke of it lies along strokes of figure 1, at some size and after turning it. Try each letter of figure 2 in turn and count those that need a stroke figure 1 does not have, such as a curve where figure 1 has only straight lines or a stroke through one of its gaps. IIT Bombay's final key gives 17 letters that cannot fit.

questions.text: Two gears A and B with red arrows are shown below. Gear A rotates in clockwise direction. How many complete rotations does the gear B have to make for the red arrows to meet?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Gear A has 11 teeth and gear B has 8. The red arrow on B is at the gap now meshing with A, and A's arrow is 3 teeth before the meshing point in A's clockwise turn. The arrows meet when A has turned k teeth with k leaving 3 over a multiple of 11 and k a multiple of 8. The smallest such k is 80, which is 80/8 = 10 complete turns of B.

questions.text: Figure 1 is an image composed of partial circles. Some cuts in the circles form the corners of triangles as shown in Figure 2. What is the total number of triangles whose three corners are formed by three circles?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Each circle has one cut, either a right angle or a 45 degree wedge. A triangle needs three circles whose cuts point exactly at each other: the edges of each cut must aim at the other two circles. Checking every set of three circles in the 10 by 6 grid in this way gives 10 right isosceles triangles, five small ones with sides of one circle spacing and five larger ones.

questions.text: There are two discs, one with numbers and other with three cut-outs as shown in the figure 1 and are overlapped as shown in figure 2. For every second, the numbered disc rotates two numbers in anti-clockwise direction and the cut-out disc rotates one number in the clockwise direction. If the arrangement at zero second is as shown in figure 2, what will be the number inside the pentagonal cut-out at 5 seconds?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Numbers run clockwise from 1 to 10. Each second the numbers turn 2 places anticlockwise and the cut-outs turn 1 place clockwise, so relative to the numbers the cut-outs move 3 places clockwise every second. The pentagon starts at 8, so after 5 seconds it shows 8 + 15 = 23, which is 3 on a 10-number dial.

questions.text: Figure 1 is formed by a black square inscribed in a white circle which in turn is inscribed in another black square of side 2 cm as shown. If a point is chosen at random inside figure 1, what is the probability that the point will be in the area shaded black?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The outer square has side 2, area 4. The circle has radius 1, area \(\pi\). The inner square fits in the circle with diagonal 2, so its area is 2. Black area = \((4 - \pi) + 2 = 6 - \pi\), about 2.858. Probability = \((6 - \pi)/4\), about 0.71.

questions.text: Two discs shown below are spun randomly and they come to rest after some time. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers in the two discs pointed by the red arrows equals seven or more?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: On the first disc 5 and 4 each cover a third and 3 and 2 each cover a sixth; on the second disc 2, 3, 4 and 5 each cover a quarter. Sum at least 7: first 5 always (1/3), first 4 needs 3 or more (1/3 x 3/4 = 1/4), first 3 needs 4 or more (1/6 x 1/2 = 1/12), first 2 needs 5 (1/6 x 1/4 = 1/24). Total = 17/24, about 0.71.

questions.text: Shown below are two views of the same 3D object. How many non-contiguous surfaces are there in the object?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Use both views to build up the object, then count its surfaces one at a time. A new surface starts at every sharp edge, so each flat face of each piece, including the faces of the small cube, counts separately. Tick each face off on the views so that none is counted twice. IIT Bombay's final key gives 36 surfaces.

questions.text: Sharmila takes the office bus home every day in the evening. She takes the five o' clock bus and gets off exactly at six o' clock at the bus stop nearest to her house. Her husband driving from home picks her up at the bus stop, and they drive back home. One day Sharmila decided to take the four o' clock bus and reached her bus stop at five o' clock. Thinking that her husband won't be able to pick her up earlier than usual, she decided to walk home. At some point during her walk, her husband picked her up and they reached home ten minutes earlier than they usually reach home. Assuming that Sharmila's husband always drives at a constant speed, and that on this occasion he left home as usual, how long (in minutes) Sharmila walked before she was picked up?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: They reached home 10 minutes early, so the husband saved 5 minutes each way. He normally reaches the stop at 6:00, so he met her at 5:55. She started walking at 5:00, so she walked for 55 minutes.

questions.text:
A 3 × 3 grid as shown in figure 1 is to be filled with numbers 1 to 9 according to the following rules:
- 8 is above 9 and to the right of 2
- 3 is to the right of 7 and above 9 which is to the left of 4
- 2 is to the left of 5
- 7 is above 6 and 2
- 1 is above 5
- ‘To the left of’ or ‘to the right of’ means in the same row
- ‘Above’ or ‘below’ means in the same column
What is the sum of the three numbers in the middle row?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: 3 and 8 are both above 9, so 3, 8, 9 fill one column top to bottom; 7 is left of 3 and above 2 and 6, 2 is left of 8 and 5, and 1 is above 5. Placing them gives top row 7, 3, 1; middle row 2, 8, 5; bottom row 6, 9, 4, which meets every rule. The middle row sums to 2 + 8 + 5 = 15.

questions.text: A greenhouse constructed in the shape of a hemi-spherical dome houses a cuboid structure as shown in the given figure. The top four corners of the cuboid just touch the inside of the hemi-sphere. The diameter of the hemi-sphere is 20 m. The centre of the base of the cuboid and the centre of the base of the hemi-sphere coincide. A ladder AB is placed from one corner of the cuboid as indicated by the point B, reaching the centre of the top surface of the cuboid as indicated by the point A. What is the length of the ladder AB?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: A top corner of the cuboid touches the dome, so its distance from the centre of the base is the radius, 10 m. If the cuboid's height is h and a base corner is at distance d from the centre, then d squared plus h squared = 100. A is h above the centre and B is at distance d on the base, so AB squared = d squared + h squared = 100 and AB = 10 m.

questions.text: Which of the sculpture(s) given below belong(s) to the Gandhara style?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Gandhara sculpture shows Greco-Roman influence: wavy hair, realistic faces, grey schist or stucco. A, a stucco head with wavy hair, and C, a bearded ascetic in grey schist, are Gandhara. B is red sandstone with snail-shell curls, the Mathura style. D, with smooth features and a decorated halo in buff sandstone, is Gupta-period Sarnath.

questions.text:
Consider a scenario in India in the year 2000: Women from several nomadic tribes are in danger of having complicated pregnancies. At times, they have little or no knowledge of pregnancy or childbirth related ailments, interventions and government schemes. The problem is worsened by the fact that women’s literacy within these communities is low and since they keep moving from place to place, access to electricity is low. An NGO decides to address this problem and hopes to improve maternal health in this community through information dissemination.

Which of the following could be effective in communicating this information to this community?
I. Smartphone applications
II. Smart watches with health monitoring sensors
III. Camps and workshops
IV. Folk songs
V. Radio
VI. Folk theatre
VII. Pregnancy tracking websites
VIII. Posters
IX. Printed booklets
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The community moves from place to place, has low literacy and little electricity, so the message must not depend on reading text or on charging devices. Folk songs and folk theatre (B) need neither; camps and workshops and the radio (C) reach people directly, and a radio runs on batteries; posters and booklets (D) work without power when they carry pictures. Smartphone apps, smart watches and websites (A) need literacy, power and connectivity, so B, C and D are correct.

questions.text: Which of the statement(s) is/are TRUE for the photos given below?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The photos show a whale shark (fish), a tortoise (reptile), a humpback whale (mammal), an owl (bird), a sloth bear (mammal), a monitor lizard (reptile), a bat (mammal) and a frog (amphibian). That is three mammals, so A is false; two reptiles, so B is true; one fish, so C is false; one bird, so D is true.

questions.text:
Somewhere, on some remote planet set at precisely the right distance from a star of just the right magnitude and the right temperature, on the other side of our galaxy, there is at this moment a committee nearing the end of a year-long study of our own tiny, provincial solar system. The intelligent beings of that place are putting their signatures (numbers of some sort, no doubt) to a paper which asserts, with finality, that life is out of the question here and the place is not worth an expedition. Their instruments have detected the presence of that most lethal of all gases, oxygen, and that is the end of that. They had planned to come, bringing along mobile factories for manufacturing life-giving ammonia, but what’s the use of risking strangulation?

The only part of this scenario that I really believe in is that committee. I take it as an article of faith that this is the most fundamental aspect of nature that we know about. If you are going to go looking for evidences of life on other celestial bodies, you need special instruments with delicate sensors for detecting the presence of committees. If there is life there, you will find consortia, collaborating groups, working parties, all over the place.

At least this is true for our kind of life.

Consider the following paragraphs:

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE of the paragraph above?

options.label: A
options.text: The author suggests that bureaucratic committees waste a lot of time before taking decisions on important projects.

options.label: B
options.text: The basic error in the passage is in the assertion that oxygen can be a lethal gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Past the veneer of sarcasm, the author admits to a deep faith in the fundamental human urge to collaborate and consort in all large endeavours.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether as numerals or symbols, the author believes in the universality of numbers as a language that transcends boundaries.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: Behind the sarcasm about the alien committee, the author says the one part he truly believes is the committee itself: life everywhere forms groups that work together, so C is true. The aside that the beings sign their report with numbers of some sort, no doubt, shows the author assuming numbers are a language any intelligent life would use, which is D. A is wrong because the author does not blame committees for delay, and B is wrong because the passage presents oxygen as lethal from the aliens' point of view, not as an error.

questions.text:
A central part of disgust’s pathology is the bifurcation of the world into the “pure” and the “impure”—the construction of a “we” who are without flaw and a “they” who are dirty, evil, and contaminating. Much bad thinking about international politics shows the traces of this pathology, as people prove all too ready to think about some group of others as black and sullied, while they themselves are on the side of the angels. We now notice that this very deep-seated human tendency is nourished by many time-honored modes of storytelling to children, which suggest that the world will be set right when some ugly and disgusting witch or monster is killed, or even cooked in her own oven. Many contemporary stories for children purvey the same worldview. We should be grateful for artists who suggest to children the world’s real complexity: the Japanese filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki, for example, whose wild and fantastic films contain a view of good and evil that is both gentler and more nuanced, in which dangers may come from such real and complex sources as decent humans’ relation to the environment; or Maurice Sendak, whose Max, in Where the Wild Things Are—which has now become an impressive film— romps with monsters that represent his own inner world and the dangerous aggression that lurks there. Nor are the monsters even entirely hideous; for the hatred of one’s own internal demons is a frequent source of the need to project them outward onto others. Stories learned in childhood become powerful constituents of the world we inhabit as adults.

Consider the following paragraph:

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE of the paragraph above?

options.label: A
options.text: The ability to feel concern and to respond with sympathy and imaginative perspective is a deep part of our evolutionary heritage.

options.label: B
options.text: Traditional storytelling often feeds a deep-seated human tendency to divide the world into binaries, such as pure-impure, us-them, etc., nurturing a pathology that needs to be brought in check.

options.label: C
options.text: Children’s stories need not be a matter of much concern, since the world of adults is complex enough to comfortably accommodate and/or mitigate the tendencies reflected in such tales.

options.label: D
options.text: Hayao Miyazaki and Maurice Sendak are held up as exemplars of a new, more nuanced kind of storytelling, that carries the possibility of a changed relationship with the self and the world.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: The paragraph says old stories feed the habit of splitting the world into pure and impure, us and them, and that this pathology shapes adults, so B is true. It praises Miyazaki and Sendak for showing children a gentler, more complex view of good and evil, so D is true. A is never discussed. C contradicts the last line, that childhood stories shape the adult world.

questions.text:
Read the three statements below, and the conclusions deduced from these statements.

Statements:
All letters of the Greek alphabet have symbol-to-sound mapping.
Some letters of the Greek alphabet are aspirated plosives.
All aspirated plosives in Greek are consonants in Greek.

Based on the above, which of the conclusions actually follows from the statements?

options.label: C
options.text: All aspirated plosives are letters of the Greek alphabet.

options.label: D
options.text: No letters of the Greek alphabet are consonants.

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Some Greek letters are aspirated plosives, and every aspirated plosive in Greek is a consonant, so those letters are consonants: some consonants are aspirated plosives (A). Those same letters, being Greek letters, have symbol-to-sound mapping, so some consonants have it (B). Nothing says every aspirated plosive is a Greek letter, so C does not follow, and D is contradicted.

questions.text: Which of the visual element(s) is/are part of the design shown below? The element(s) may be rotated or scaled.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.subtopic: Matching a part to the whole
questions.solution: Look at each coloured piece of the design and compare its outline with each element, after turning and resizing the element. Each of A, B, C and D matches a piece of the design: a curved strip, a fan shape with bumps, and the other shaped pieces beside the arches. So all four are part of the design.

questions.text: Which of the figure(s) can be drawn by neither lifting the pen nor redrawing the line?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A figure can be drawn in one stroke without retracing if it is connected and at most two points have an odd number of lines meeting. Ordinary crossings have 4 lines, which is even. In B and D one extra curve starts or ends at a crossing, giving exactly two points where 5 lines meet, so they can be drawn starting at one and ending at the other. A is one continuous scribble. C has four points where 5 lines meet, so it cannot be drawn.

questions.text: Shown below is a design pattern. Which of the given option(s) can be used as blocks to print the given pattern?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A printing block prints its own mirror image, and blocks may be turned and repeated. Check whether repeating each block, turned or flipped as needed, gives the pattern's wavy lines with the same thicknesses in the same order. IIT Bombay's final key accepts all four blocks.

questions.text: Shown below are fractal images generated by the repetition and scaling of basic units (shown next to the fractal). Which of the option(s) has/have the correct basic unit?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Look at the smallest branches of each fractal and compare them with the unit drawn beside it: the repeated unit must have the same angles between its parts and the same number of branches. In C and D the fractal is built from copies of the given unit; in A and B the branches meet at different angles or split differently from the unit.

questions.text: Shown below is a print roller. Which of the given option(s) is/are partly or fully printed using the roller?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.subtopic: Matching a part to the whole
questions.solution: Only the raised arcs on the rim (drawn thick) touch the paper, so going round the roller gives a fixed cyclic order of black bars and white gaps. Measured in small units the rim reads: bar 1, gap 4, bar 6, gap 2, bar 2, gap 1, bar 1, gap 6, bar 4, gap 2, bar 2, gap 1, bar 1, gap 2, bar 2, gap 2, bar 1, gap 1, bar 2, gap 2, bar 4, gap 1, and then it repeats. A, B and C are each an unbroken stretch of this sequence. D starts like the stretch after the widest bar but then shows a gap of 4 and a thin bar where the roller has a gap of 6 followed by a bar of 4, so it cannot come from the roller.

questions.text: Shown below is a wooden partition with hinges along KK, LL, MM, NN and OO. The partitions are folded in such a way that only two panels are to be visible side by side at any time. Which of the given option(s) showing the folds is/are possible?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Number the six panels 1 to 6 from left to right. Option A shows panels 3 and 5, B shows 1 and 6, C shows 2 and 5 and D shows 2 and 4. Panels hidden between the two visible ones must fold back behind them and return to the same seam, which needs an even number of hidden panels (one folds back, the next folds forward). B hides 4 panels and C hides 2, so both work; A and D each hide one panel between them, which would leave a gap of one panel width.

questions.text:
Consider the following paragraph:
“Imagine a gigantic banquet. Hundreds of millions of people come to eat. They eat and drink to their hearts’ content—eating food that is better and more abundant than at the finest tables in ancient Athens or Rome, or even in the palaces of medieval Europe. Then, one day, a man arrives, wearing a white dinner jacket. He says he is holding the bill. Not surprisingly, the diners are in shock. Some begin to deny that this is their bill. Others deny that there even is a bill. Still others deny that they partook of the meal. One diner suggests that the man is not really a waiter, but is only trying to get attention for himself or to raise money for his own projects. Finally, the group concludes that if they simply ignore the waiter, he will go away. This is where we stand today on the subject of global warming. For the past 150 years, industrial civilization has been dining on the energy stored in fossil fuels, and the bill has come due. Yet, we have sat around the dinner table denying that it is our bill, and doubting the credibility of the man who delivered it.”

So said Naomi Oreskes in “Merchants of Doubt”.
Which of the statements reflect/s the author’s position:

options.label: A
options.text: Global warming is due to our usage of fossil fuels.

options.label: B
options.text: Global warming may not be man-made, but it is still real.

options.label: C
options.text: Some are sceptical of what science is telling us about global warming.

options.label: D
options.text: Some are not willing to take responsibility for global warming.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: The author says industrial civilization has been dining on the energy in fossil fuels and the bill has come due, so A is her position. The diners who doubt the credibility of the man delivering the bill stand for people sceptical of the science, so C fits. Those who deny it is their bill are refusing responsibility, so D fits. B contradicts the passage, which treats warming as the bill for our own fossil fuel use, that is, man-made.

questions.text: Given below are images of sculpture, furniture and buildings. Which of the statement(s) is/are TRUE for the images given below?

options.label: A
options.text: M and L are by the same designer

options.label: B
options.text: P and Q are by the same designer

options.label: C
options.text: L and N are by the same designer

options.label: D
options.text: P and R are by same architect

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: L is the Palace of Assembly at Chandigarh and M is the Open Hand monument there, both by Le Corbusier, so A is true. P is Alvar Aalto's main building at Otaniemi (Helsinki University of Technology) and Q is his tea trolley, so B is true. N is Frank Lloyd Wright's barrel chair, not Le Corbusier's, so C is false. R is Wright's Fallingwater, not Aalto's, so D is false.

questions.text: Which of the statement(s) is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Agricultural activities and use of fertilizers leads to higher nitrous oxide concentration

options.label: B
options.text: Deforestation leads to decrease in carbon dioxide due to human activities

options.label: C
options.text: Oxygen and ozone are not greenhouse gases

options.label: D
options.text: Global warming leads to sea level rise

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Nitrogen fertilizers and farming are the largest human source of nitrous oxide, so A is true. Warming melts land ice and expands sea water, so sea level rises and D is true. Deforestation removes trees that take in carbon dioxide and releases the carbon they store, so it increases carbon dioxide and B is false. IIT Bombay's final key gives A, C and D.
questions.defect: Statement C is false as printed: ozone is a greenhouse gas (oxygen is not). IIT Bombay's final key counts C as true.

questions.text: Which of the pieces given below can be joined together to form a complete cube?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Piece D is a corner of the cube: three full edges meet at right angles and a single slanted cut removes the rest. Piece A is a block whose top is the full square face with one corner cut off, standing on a slanted cut that runs from one top corner down towards the opposite bottom corner. Piece C is a right angled triangular wedge. Estimating volumes from the drawings, A is about half the cube, D about a third and C about a sixth, which together make one cube; B adds volume that has no place left.

questions.text: Given all the batteries in the circuits shown below are of same voltage and all the bulbs are of same wattage, and the internal resistance is negligible in all the cases, which of the statement(s) is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Bulbs in circuit Q and R will have same intensity

options.label: B
options.text: Bulbs in circuit P and R will have same intensity

options.label: C
options.text: Bulb in circuit Q will be the brightest

options.label: D
options.text: Bulb in circuit S will not glow

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: P has one cell, so the bulb gets voltage V. Q has two cells in series, positive to negative, so the bulb gets 2V and is the brightest. R has two cells in parallel, which still give V, so P and R glow equally and Q and R do not. In S the two cells face each other with like poles joined, so their voltages cancel and the bulb does not glow.

questions.text: Figure 1 shows an unfolded view of a box. The dotted lines depict the folding lines. The options show four fully folded boxes. Identify the box(es) that can be unfolded as figure 1?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Fold the net with the lower middle rhombus (tan band) as the front. Then the upper middle rhombus is the top (green on its right half), the top left piece is the left face (blue on its lower half), the top right piece is the back (blue on the half next to the left face), the bottom left piece is the bottom (green on its back half) and the bottom right piece is the right face (tan on its back half). Looking at the back, bottom and right faces together gives A: green and tan bands both run along the blue face, and the blue band runs along the hidden side. Looking at the front, left and top faces gives D: blue and tan bands both run along the hidden side next to green, and the green band runs along the hidden bottom. In B and in C a band runs along a face whose own band does not match the net, so they cannot be folded from it.

questions.text: When force is applied on arms P and Q in the direction indicated by the arrows, R and S move away from each other. When that force is removed, R and S fall back towards each other. Which of the option(s) satisfies (satisfy) the above condition?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Squeezing P and Q together opens R and S; for R and S to close again on their own, the joint at the end of P and Q must push the arms apart once the force is removed, so it must store energy like a spring. B is a bent spring strip, as in a pair of tongs, and D is a coiled torsion spring, as in a clothes peg, so both spring back. A is a plain pin joint and C is a set of pin jointed links, which move freely but give no restoring force, so R and S would stay apart.

questions.text: Which of the option(s) given below can fit in the empty box?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Every box holds six shapes. Across each row the number of circles rises by one and the number of triangles falls by one: row 1 has circles 3, 4, 5 and triangles 3, 2, 1; row 2 has 2, 3, 4 and 4, 3, 2; row 3 has 1, 2 and 5, 4. Down each column the circles fall by one. So the empty box needs 3 circles and 3 triangles. A has 3 circles and 3 triangles, and so does C. B has only 2 circles and 2 triangles, and D has 4 circles and 4 triangles.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about sound?

options.label: A
options.text: As you tighten a drum skin, the sound made when you beat it gets lower in pitch.

options.label: B
options.text: As the water level in a bottle increases, the sound made when you blow over the top of it gets lower in pitch.

options.label: C
options.text: As the water level in a bottle decreases, the sound you make when you tap on the mouth, periodically gets lower in pitch.

options.label: D
options.text: When you hit a steel plate to make a loud sound and then hold the edge of the plate tightly between your fingers, the sound becomes higher in pitch.

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: A tighter drum skin vibrates faster, so its pitch rises: A is false. Blowing over a bottle sounds the air column above the water; more water means a shorter column and a higher pitch, so B is false. Tapping on the mouth of the bottle also sounds that air column: less water means a longer column and a lower pitch, so C is true. Gripping the edge of a struck steel plate clamps it, so it can only vibrate in its faster modes and the sound becomes higher in pitch, so D is true.

questions.text: Shown below are photographs of same objects using different settings. Given that the lighting conditions were constant in all, which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: All the photographs are of equal exposure

options.label: B
options.text: The third photograph was taken with a moving camera

options.label: C
options.text: The photographs are in the order of small to large aperture size

options.label: D
options.text: The third photograph was taken with a higher shutter-speed compared to the first photograph

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The three photographs are equally bright, so they have equal exposure (A). The depth of field shrinks from the first to the third: in the first almost every sweet is sharp, in the third only the red ones are, so the aperture grows from small to large (C). With the light unchanged, a larger aperture lets in more light, so to keep the same exposure the third needs a faster shutter than the first (D). The blur in the third is the even blur of shallow focus around a sharp subject, not the streaking of a moving camera, so B is false.

questions.text: When photographs are taken on bright sunny days, there is a possibility of an intense glare appearing in the photograph. Which action(s) can be taken to avoid the glare?

options.label: A
options.text: Change the angle of the camera

options.label: B
options.text: Open up the aperture to its maximum

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Changing the camera angle keeps direct sunlight and strong reflections out of the lens (A). A lens hood shades the front of the lens from stray sunlight (C). A polarizing filter cuts the polarised light reflected from shiny surfaces such as water and glass (D). Opening the aperture to its maximum only lets in more light, which makes glare worse, so B does not help.

questions.text: Which of the option(s) describe(s) the films shown below in the correct order?

options.label: A
options.text: Animation, Adventure, Interview, Fantasy, Comedy, Documentary

options.label: B
options.text: Comedy, Adventure, Documentary, Science-Fiction, Mystery, Action

options.label: C
options.text: Animation, Adventure, Documentary, Action, Film Noir, War

options.label: D
options.text: Comedy, Drama, Action, Science-Fiction, Romance, Thriller

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Still 1 is from Toy Story (an animated comedy), 2 from Life of Pi (adventure), 3 is an interview with Barack Obama (documentary), 4 a lightsaber duel from Star Wars (science fiction action), 5 a black and white silhouette scene (film noir, mystery) and 6 from Saving Private Ryan (war, action). B and C name a fitting genre for every still in order. A calls the noir still a comedy and the war film a documentary, and D calls the interview action and the noir still romance, so both fail.

questions.text: Shown on the left is the logo of Beijing Olympics. Which of the pictogram(s) was/were used in the same Olympics?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The Beijing 2008 pictograms are based on ancient Chinese seal script: a white figure drawn with brush-like strokes on a black square with a rough, stamped edge. A and C are from that set. B and D only resemble it: their figures are drawn in a different style, so they belong to other Games.

questions.text:
Read the poem given below and identify the Rasa in it.

Ashadha’s ending on the mountain found
Him weakened, gold ring slipping from his wrist,
And mixed his pleasure when a cloud came down
So playfully to hug the summit mist,
As elephants in heat will butt the ground.

In tears withheld he took that fall from grace,
From wealth attending on the King of Kings.
The otherworld that brimmed in cloudy air
Was still discomfort when far longing brings
A breath to hold him to that neck’s embrace.

With now the rainy month stood close at hand,
To fresh Kutaja blooms he adds his plea
And asks most courteously the cloud bring news
Of welfare to his loved-one—words that she,
Revived to hear of him, will understand.
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The lines are from Kalidasa's Meghaduta: an exiled yaksha, weakened by separation, longs for his beloved and asks a cloud to carry news of his welfare to her. Longing for an absent lover is Shringara rasa in its separation form (vipralambha). There is no heroism (Veera), humour (Hasya) or astonishment (Adbhuta) at the centre of the poem.

questions.text: An oxymoron is a figure of speech in which contradictory images or words are juxtaposed in order to intensify a statement or to produce a heightened poetic effect. Which of the statements given below is NOT an oxymoron?

options.label: A
options.text: We eat in order to live, not live in order to eat.

options.label: B
options.text: Still-waking sleep, that is not what it is!

options.label: C
options.text: No light, but rather darkness visible.

options.label: D
options.text: To that bad eminence; and from despair.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: An oxymoron joins two words that contradict each other. 'Still-waking sleep' pairs waking with sleep, 'darkness visible' pairs darkness with being seen, and 'bad eminence' pairs bad with a word of high honour, so B, C and D are oxymorons. A only reverses the order of the same words (eat to live, live to eat), which is a chiasmus, not an oxymoron.

questions.text: Identify the option that will replace the question mark.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Call the faces W (wink with tongue), S (plain smile), X (squinting with tongue) and L (squinting laugh). The rows read W S X L W, S W L X S, X L W S X, L ? S W L, W S X L W. Row 2 is row 1 with each neighbouring pair swapped, and row 4 must likewise be row 3 with pairs swapped: X L W S becomes L X S W. The grid is also the same read down the columns as across the rows, and column 2 reads S W L ? S, matching row 2 (S W L X S). Both give X, the squinting face with tongue out, which is A.

questions.text: Shape P is folded along the dotted lines to form shape Q and then folded again to form shape R. Identify the pattern on the backside of P.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Folding the four outer flaps onto the diamond gives Q, and folding the four tips of the diamond to the centre gives R, so every mark seen on R lies on the back of P near one of the diamond's corners. A tip folded down from the top or up from the bottom turns its marks upside down, while a tip folded in from the side only swaps sides when P is turned over. So the blue tick sits just inside the top with the curved line below it, the smile appears upside down as a frown just inside the bottom with the curve above it, the orange half disc with its curve sits at the left corner and the green dot with its curve at the right corner. That is pattern B.

questions.text: An image strip is cut into four pieces. Identify the correct sequence that will complete the image correctly.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.subtopic: Matching a part to the whole
questions.solution: The white moon cut at the right edge of P continues at the left edge of S, so S follows P. The cloud bands at the right edge of S continue into the left edge of Q, so Q follows S. The left edge of P continues the curling clouds and the dark line at the right edge of R, while R's left edge does not join Q's right edge, so R comes first: R, P, S, Q.

questions.text: Identify the option that will replace the question mark.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Follow each object across the three boxes. The clock colour moves through the rainbow: orange, yellow, green, so blue comes next. The motorbike turns to face the other way in each box: right, left, right, so it must face left next. The pencil grows a little each time, so it is a step larger than in the third box rather than very large. Only C has a blue clock, a left facing motorbike and a pencil one step larger; A and D have the bike facing right and colours out of order, and B has a red clock.

questions.text: Each of the shapes is associated with one or more alphabets. Identify the alphabet(s) for the last shape.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Each shape is named by the letter whose position in the alphabet equals its number of sides: the triangle (3) is C, the hexagon (6) is F, the octagon (8) is H, and an octagon holding a square (8 and 4) is HD. The last shape has a top edge, two slanted edges and a short straight neck on each side, and a bottom edge, which is 8 sides, so it is H.

questions.text: Identify the option that will replace the question mark.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The red hand is the hour hand and the black hand the minute hand. The clocks show 9:00, 9:00 again, 3:00, ?, 7:30. The jumps halve each time: 9:00 plus 12 hours is 9:00, plus 6 hours is 3:00, plus 3 hours is 6:00, plus one and a half hours is 7:30. So the missing clock shows 6:00, with the hour hand pointing down and the minute hand up, which is B.

questions.text: The object shown below is rotated by 180 degrees about the X axis in the anticlockwise direction as seen from the top. Identify the trail left by the orange blobs when seen from the top.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Each blob sweeps half a circle around the vertical axis, with radius equal to its distance from the axis. Where a blob on the left and a blob on the right sit at the same distance, the two halves join into a full circle. Measuring the blobs, the one on the axis leaves a dot, nine distances have a blob on both sides and give full circles, the farthest left blob has no partner and gives the outermost half circle, and the small inner blob on the right has no partner and gives a half circle second from the centre. Turning anticlockwise seen from above, the left blob sweeps through the near (lower) half and the right blob through the far (upper) half. B shows exactly this: a dot, an upper half circle second from the centre, nine full circles and an outer lower half circle.

questions.text: Which shape will exactly fit with Figure 1 without leaving any gaps, given that the shapes can be rotated?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Turn Figure 1 upside down and place its side against a curved side of A: every bulge of the vase (the rim, the wide shoulder, the small knob near the base) lands in a matching hollow of A, so the two outlines lock together with no gap. B, C and D are one other shape drawn at different angles; their curved sides are close to Figure 1's outline but the bumps sit at slightly different heights, so they leave gaps.

questions.text: A cube, a cuboid, a cone and a sphere were developed from an experimental material. In vacuum, the combined mass of the cuboid and the sphere is equivalent to the combined mass of the cube and the cone. The mass of the cuboid is equivalent to the combined mass of the sphere and the cone. The sphere weighed 2 kilograms and occupied a volume of 62.5 cubic cm in vacuum. One of the properties of this material is such that the length of the side of the cube doubles when exposed to air. How many cubes are needed to fill a tank of dimension 50 cm x 50 cm x 50 cm in air?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Cuboid + sphere = cube + cone, and cuboid = sphere + cone, so sphere + cone + sphere = cube + cone, giving cube = 2 sphere = 4 kg. The material has 2 kg per 62.5 cubic cm, so the 4 kg cube has volume 125 cubic cm and side 5 cm. In air the side doubles to 10 cm, so the 50 cm tank holds 5 cubes along each edge: 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 cubes.

questions.text: Shown below are the different views of the same ball. Identify its top view.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: In the front view the seam runs from the very top of the ball down its middle, so the seam passes over the top point of the ball and through the centre of the top view. At mid height the front view shows the seam just right of centre, so in the top view the seam meets the front (lower) edge slightly right of centre. The right view shows the seam crossing the middle height towards the back, so in the top view it meets the right edge above the middle. Only option A has a seam that enters at the bottom just right of centre, passes the centre and leaves through the upper part of the right edge.

questions.text: Identify the odd one out.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Each circle holds five coloured strips with seven crossings. In A, C and D exactly one strip (the yellow one) crosses all four others, and the remaining four strips form a simple chain of crossings. In B two strips, the purple and the yellow, each cross all the other strips, so its crossing pattern is different. B is the odd one out.

questions.text: The enclosed yellow shape within the letter ‘b’ is called a counter. Which option has the red shape as the counter?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The red counter is a fairly upright rounded shape, about 1.3 times as tall as it is wide, with flattish sides. Comparing the enclosed white space inside each ‘p’: A's counter is narrower and taller, C's is slightly tilted and taller, D's is rounder at the top. The counter of B has the same proportions and outline as the red shape.

questions.text: Shown below is a schematic figure of two rows of test tubes with the ground shadows seen from the top. The test tubes are of varying heights. Identify the set of test tubes that cast the shadows.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: All shadows fall at the same angle, so a longer shadow means a taller tube, and a front tube's shadow runs along the same diagonal as the back tube one place to its right. The top view shows long shadows on the 2nd, 4th and 5th diagonals, a medium one from the first back tube, a short one on the 3rd diagonal and a short one from the last front tube. Option D has tall tubes on those three diagonals (back tube 2, front tube 3, back tube 5), a medium first back tube and short front tubes 2 and 5.

questions.text: A naughty kid plays with a clock kept on a table as shown below. She changes the hour and minute hands clockwise adding 8 hours and 45 minutes to the time and places the clock by rotating 270 degrees anti-clock wise. Identify the option that shows the modified time?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The clock shows about 1:40 (short hand between 1 and 2, long hand at 8). Adding 8 hours 45 minutes gives 10:25, so the short hand points just past 10 and the long hand points at 5. Turning the clock 270 degrees anticlockwise is the same as 90 degrees clockwise, which moves the short hand to between 1 and 2 and the long hand to 8 on the table. The frame is also turned a quarter turn clockwise, and only D shows the frame in that position with these hands.

questions.text: In 2001, one lakh people (10% of the total population) of a city used private vehicles and 50% of the population used public transportation. In 2011, there was a decadal growth of 10% and it was observed that five lakh people used public transportation, while 2 lakh people used private vehicles. Which pie chart depicts the transportation mode usage in 2011?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: One lakh is 10% of the 2001 population, so the population was 10 lakh. With 10% growth the 2011 population is 11 lakh. Public transport is 5/11, about 46%, private vehicles 2/11, about 18%, and others 4/11, about 36%. Pie chart B shows Public 46%, Private 18%, Others 36%.

questions.text: In a school of 600 students, 10% played football, hockey and cricket while 60 were engaged in other sports. 18% of the students played football while 90 played cricket exclusively. 60 students played both football and cricket. 66 students played hockey exclusively and another 11% played both hockey and cricket. Which option represents the school?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The diagrams are in percentages of 600. All three games: 10%; other sports 60, which is 10%; football only 18%; cricket only 90, which is 15%; football and cricket 60, which is 10%; hockey only 66, which is 11%; hockey and cricket 11%. The remaining football and hockey region is 100 minus 85, which is 15%. Diagram C shows cricket 15, football 18, hockey 11, football and cricket 10, cricket and hockey 11, centre 10, football and hockey 15 and outside 10.

questions.text: A cube of side 10 cm is merged with a square pyramid of base 10 cm and height 15 cm. The centers of the base for both the objects are aligned. Identify the top view of the resultant figure from the options given below.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The pyramid's base is turned 45 degrees to the cube, so its corners poke out beyond the middle of each side of the cube as small triangles, with the sloping edge to the apex seen as a line through each. The pyramid is taller than the cube, so its top 5 cm shows above the cube's top face as a small diamond with its four edges meeting at the apex. The rest of the pyramid's base lies under the cube's top face and cannot be seen. Option B shows exactly this.

questions.text:
Following operations, in the given order have been performed on the figure shown in the box.
i. Rotate 180°
ii. Flip horizontal (about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the computer screen)
iii. Rotate 180°
iv. Flip vertical (about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the computer screen)

Identify the resultant figure.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Take each flip as a mirror flip. The two 180 degree rotations cancel each other, and a horizontal flip followed by a vertical flip is the same as a 180 degree rotation. So the four steps together turn the figure through 180 degrees, which is option A.

questions.text: If gear ‘P’ is the driving gear and rotates clockwise, which of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Q will rotate clockwise and S will rotate anticlockwise

options.label: B
options.text: R and T both will rotate anticlockwise

options.label: C
options.text: R will rotate clockwise and U will rotate anticlockwise

options.label: D
options.text: S will rotate anticlockwise and U will rotate clockwise

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Two gears on opposite sides of a rack turn in opposite directions, and two meshing gears also turn in opposite directions. P (clockwise) and Q are on opposite sides of the first rack, so Q turns anticlockwise. Q and R are on opposite sides of the second rack, so R turns clockwise; S meshes with R, so S turns anticlockwise. S and T are on opposite sides of the third rack, so T turns clockwise, and U meshes with T, so U turns anticlockwise. Only C (R clockwise, U anticlockwise) is true.

questions.text: The image in the box on the left hand side shows the open and closed positions for a metal stand. The other two images show the various joints in the stand. If a fixed joint is denoted by ‘f’ and a hinged joint is denoted by ‘h’ then which of the options is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: P-f ; Q-h ; R-f ; S-h ; T-h ; U-f ; V-f

options.label: B
options.text: P-h ; Q-h ; R-h ; S-f ; T-h ; U-f ; V-h

options.label: C
options.text: P-f ; Q-h ; R-f ; S-h ; T-h ; U-h ; V-h

options.label: D
options.text: P-f ; Q-h ; R-f ; S-f ; T-h ; U-h ; V-h

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The two front legs keep the same spread when the stand closes, so their top joints P and R and the crossbar joint S are fixed. Only the back leg swings, so its top joint Q is a hinge. The brace from the crossbar to the back leg must fold as the back leg comes forward, so it is hinged where it meets the crossbar (T), in its middle (U) and at the back leg (V). That is option D.

questions.text: Three holes have been drilled through a cube of size 5 x 5 x 5 units. From the options given, identify the form that can fill the holes perfectly?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Follow each hole into the cube from its opening and note how many cubes deep it runs and where it turns, using the openings on the top, left and right faces. The filling piece must have exactly the same path, so match each option's arms and bends against it. IIT Bombay's final key gives A.

questions.text: The image in the box given below shows a 3D object. Only one of the options shows the same object from a different view. Identify it.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Note the object's arms in the box: where each one starts, which way it turns and how long it is. Turn the object in your mind to each option's viewpoint and check every arm. Option B shows the same object from another side; each of the others has one arm turned the wrong way or too long.

questions.text:
Given below is a list of ten idioms with animal/bird/fish/insect origins. Each of the four options contains four meanings. Identify the option that contains four correct meanings for any four of the idioms.
I. The elephant in the room
II. Hold your horses
III. Pig headed
IV. Wild goose chase
V. Wolf down
VI. Red herring
VII. Go to the dogs
VIII. Hogwash
IX. Sacred cow
X. Clam up

options.label: D
options.text: Be patient, recalcitrant, clean up, protected interest

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: Pig headed means obstinate, a wild goose chase is a foolish pursuit, a red herring is a misleading distraction (a subterfuge), and hogwash means rubbish, so all four meanings in C are correct. A fails on brave attempt, which matches none of the idioms. B fails on too big (the elephant in the room is an obvious problem nobody mentions). D fails on clean up (to clam up is to fall silent).

questions.text:
Choose the set of words that will correctly complete the following five sentences from the word sets given in the options
I. He (lays / lies) the book on the table.
II. The new rules (affected / effected) positive changes in the school.
III. The road through the mountains was (tortuous / torturous).
IV. The nurse was able to (staunch / stanch) the bleeding.
V. When rain threatens, fans are (reticent / reluctant) to buy tickets to the cricket match.
questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: He lays the book (lay takes an object; lie does not). The rules effected changes, meaning brought them about. A winding road is tortuous; torturous means painful. To stop bleeding is to stanch it; staunch is the adjective meaning loyal. Fans unwilling to buy are reluctant; reticent means unwilling to speak. That is option D.

questions.text: Our natural ______________ to focus on the unusual, the dramatic and the _________ is strengthened ______________ by newspapers and other media, but our interest __________ quickly as well.
questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: The first blank needs a tendency to focus on something, so aversion and dislike are wrong. The word but signals a contrast with strengthened, so our interest must fade quickly, which rules out increases and intensifies. Proclivity (a natural tendency), new, immeasurably and wanes fit every blank, so C is correct.

questions.text: Identify the option that will bisect the given shape into two identical shapes.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Count the grid squares: the shape has 26, so each half must have 13. Turn line B a quarter turn clockwise so its short arm runs one square across and its long arm three squares down. Start it at the left edge of the top block, one square below the top, and drop it to the bottom edge. The left piece and the right piece then each have 13 squares and are the same shape, one being the other turned around. None of the other lines, at the size drawn, can cut the shape into two equal 13-square pieces.

questions.text: Shown below are two metal bolts. Suppose they were to be rotated (at the same rate) in the two directions as shown by the two arrows respectively, what would happen to the distance between the two bolt heads?

options.label: B
options.text: Move farther apart from each other

options.label: C
options.text: Remain at the same distance from each other

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Both arrows turn their bolts the same way in space: the near side of each bolt moves up and the far side moves down. Both bolts carry the same (right-hand) thread, so turning them the same way makes the thread pattern of each slide sideways at the same speed and in the same direction. Where the threads touch, the crests of one stay in the grooves of the other without either bolt having to move along its length. So the heads stay the same distance apart.

questions.text: Three positions X, Y and Z are marked on the cutting edges of a pair of scissors as shown. Rank the points in terms of cutting strength from strongest to weakest.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Scissors are a pair of levers turning about the pivot screw, with the effort applied at the handles. For the same effort, the force at the blade is larger the closer the point is to the pivot, because its lever arm is shorter. X is nearest the pivot and Z is farthest, so the order from strongest to weakest is X, Y, Z.

questions.text: The shapes given in the options can be used to cut figure 1 into a number of identical pieces. Which shape will cut figure 1 such that, all four symbols are included in each of the pieces, and no symbols are left over?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Figure 1 has 32 squares, 8 of each symbol, so it must be cut into 8 four-square pieces, each holding one spade, one heart, one club and one diamond. Working from the top-left corner, the T-shaped piece B can be placed, turned as needed, so that every piece holds all four symbols and the whole figure is used, in exactly one way. With the L shapes A and C or the step shape D, every attempt leaves a piece with a repeated symbol or a square that cannot be covered.

questions.text: The given figure 1 is cut into pieces. Identify the option whose pieces can be correctly assembled to form the figure 1.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Take the bar width of the H as one unit: the H is two 5-unit bars joined by a 2-unit crossbar, 12 squares in all. In A the two top pieces fit together into a 1 by 4 strip, which with one small square makes the left bar. The other three slanted pieces fit together into a 4-unit strip with a 2-unit stem, which with the second small square becomes the right bar with the crossbar sticking out from its middle. D has only 11 squares, and B contains a large triangle too wide to fit inside any arm of the H.

questions.text: Below is an animation sequence of Raju playing with his hair. However except Frame no.1 all others seem to be mixed up. Choose the correct order.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: In frame 6 the hair has slipped onto his forehead and he looks annoyed. In 5 he blows hard at it, in 4 the hair has flown up and his lips are still pursed, and in 8 the hair is still up but his mouth has relaxed. Then it falls back step by step: flicking out in 2, dropping over the eye in 7 and covering the eye in 3. So the order is 1, 6, 5, 4, 8, 2, 7, 3.

questions.text: An angry bird is flying in front of a pin-hole camera as seen in the picture below. If it flies back in the opposite direction, what would be the image cast on the inner wall of the camera?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Flying back the other way, the bird faces left, with its beak on the left. A pin-hole camera forms an image that is upside down and also reversed left to right, which is the same as turning the picture through 180 degrees. Turning a left-facing bird through 180 degrees puts it upside down with its beak on the right, as in B. C is the image of the bird as originally drawn, and A and D are not inverted.

questions.text:
A short interview is being planned for live TV as described below:
“We start with establishing the interview space, then close-up of the interviewer who introduces the interviewee. As the interview continues we shift between both of them as the questions are answered. After three questions, we end the interview showing both of them in the frame and then close with showing the interview space.”
For filming it, four cameras 1, 2, 3 and 4 have been placed as seen in the image below. From the options given, choose the sequence that was most closely followed.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Camera 2 has the widest view and shows the whole interview space, so it opens and closes the programme. Camera 3 frames both chairs, so it gives the shot of the two together at the end. Camera 4 is aimed at the person on the left holding the notes, the interviewer, and camera 1 at the guest on the right. So the order is 2, then 4 for the introduction, then 1 and 4 in turn through the three questions and answers, then 3 and finally 2, which is option D.

questions.text: Two different views of a solid object are shown below. If viewed from a different direction as the arrows suggest, what would the view be?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The solid has square faces and triangular faces, each square surrounded by four triangles and each triangle by three squares (a cuboctahedron). Looking straight at a square face, you see that square in the middle with a triangle on each of its four sides; the four neighbouring squares meet it only at its corners and are seen edge on, so they add nothing to the outline. Each triangle then reaches out half the square's width, so the diamond outline is exactly twice the width of the central square. That matches C; A has triangles that are too long, and B and D show extra faces that cannot be seen from this direction.

questions.text: Ida is standing on the structure as shown below. She wants to reach points A, B or C, but she can only travel on a continuous surface. Which of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Ida will be able to reach only A and B

options.label: B
options.text: Ida will be able to reach only C

options.label: C
options.text: Ida will be able to reach only A and C

options.label: D
options.text: Ida will be able to reach only A

questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Trace the surfaces from the bar Ida stands on. The tall post that carries A bends smoothly at its foot into the long bar that runs to C, so A and C are joined by one continuous surface and any route that reaches one reaches the other. The bar to B meets the rest of the frame only at sharp corners from Ida's side, so she cannot walk onto it. Ida can reach A and C only.

questions.text: Water is kept in four identical beakers but made of four different materials—shiny tin, matt black tin, shiny stainless steel and blue colour plastic. When kept under the sun, with the same amounts of water and for the same amount of time, water in which of the beakers will be the hottest?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: A matt black surface absorbs almost all the sunlight that falls on it, and tin, a metal, passes that heat quickly to the water. Shiny tin and shiny stainless steel reflect much of the sunlight away. Plastic absorbs some light but conducts heat poorly. So the water in the matt black tin beaker gets the hottest.

questions.text: Shown below is a one point perspective drawing where all the blocks except one share the same converging point. Identify the block.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: In one point perspective, the edges that run away from the viewer on every block point to a single vanishing point. Extending the receding edges of A, B and D, they all meet near one point below and between the blocks. The receding edges of C are drawn parallel to each other, so they never meet, and they do not point to that vanishing point. C is the odd block.

questions.text: Below is a set of pictures that show the variety of domes used in Islamic architecture in India. Select the order in which the design of the domes were developed, from the 13th to the 18th centuries CE.
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The earliest Sultanate tombs were roofed with a pyramid (iii). Next came low, plain domes such as those of the Tughlaq period (ii), and then Lodi period domes raised a little higher with a more decorated finial (i). The Mughals developed the bulbous dome rising from a band of petals (iv), and later Mughal and regional buildings of the 18th century used the full onion dome with a tall finial (v). So the order is iii, ii, i, iv, v.
